clinician.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old woman was admitted with electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic acidosis), skin hyperpigmentation, vomiting, weight loss, and exacerbated chronic renal failure. The clinical presentation raised suspicion of adrenal insufficiency. While serum cortisol and ACTH levels were ordered, their results were not documented. Testing for adrenal autoantibodies, including 21-hydroxylase antibodies, was performed and was positive, confirming autoimmune adrenalitis as the underlying cause.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: The patient presented with electrolyte imbalances (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis), skin hyperpigmentation, weight loss, vomiting, and chronic renal failure exacerbation.
Positive anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies confirmed autoimmune adrenalitis.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Psychiatric evaluation was considered but autoimmune adrenalitis was confirmed by positive adrenal antibodies.

remaining_uncertainties: Serum cortisol and plasma ACTH levels are not documented to confirm hormonal adrenal insufficiency.
No adrenal imaging or biopsy results are available.
Clinical course and response to treatment are not reported.
